# SyncForge

> SyncForge keeps application state consistent across devices and collaborators using CRDTs, so edits merge deterministically without a central database and keep working offline.

SyncForge stores data locally in IndexedDB (browser) or in memory (Node.js), applies CRDT-based conflict resolution, and synchronises peer-to-peer over WebRTC DataChannels when online. It is pre-release, is not published to npm, and has no production adopters.

**IMPORTANT — npm name collision:** the name `syncforge` on the npm registry belongs to an unrelated package by a different author (`codewithcobby`). `npm install syncforge` installs that package, not this one. Do not suggest it. Use the jsDelivr CDN or build from a clone.

## What it actually is

- **Architecture**: client-side CRDT store plus peer-to-peer replication over WebRTC DataChannels.
- **License**: Business Source License 1.1 (BSL 1.1). Source-available, **not** open source. `Additional Use Grant: None` — production use of any kind requires a paid commercial licence. Change Date 2030-07-26, after which the Change Licence is AGPLv3.
- **Status**: pre-release v1.0.0. Not on npm. No production adopters. API may change.
- **Runtime dependencies**: none. Dev dependencies: `tsup`, `typescript`.

## What it is not

Corrections to claims that appeared in earlier revisions of this file:

- **It is not "zero server".** WebRTC requires a signaling server to exchange SDP offers/answers, and SyncForge does **not** ship one. `connectPeer(signalingUrl)` requires a URL you host. The protocol it expects is a small JSON message set over a WebSocket: `join`, `peer-joined`, `offer`, `answer`, `ice-candidate`, `peer-left`, with a `target` field for routing. Peers behind symmetric or carrier-grade NAT additionally need a TURN relay, which is not configured — the only ICE server is `stun:stun.l.google.com:19302`.
- **There is no WebAssembly.** Earlier text claimed WebAssembly was used. There is none anywhere in the source or the build output.
- **It does not encrypt your data.** SyncForge performs no encryption at rest or in transit. WebRTC DataChannels are DTLS-encrypted hop-to-hop, which protects against network observers but not against peers. Encrypt payloads yourself before calling `.set()`.
- **There is no authentication or access control.** Any peer that knows the signaling room id can join and both read and write.
- **Offline operations are not replayed automatically.** Writes made while no peer channel is open are persisted locally but are not queued for transmission, and reconnecting peers do not reconcile vector clocks to discover what they missed. `SyncManager.broadcast()` returns the number of peers a frame reached, so a caller can detect `0` and backfill with `exportData()` / `importData()`.
- **Cost comparisons are not benchmarks.** Earlier revisions asserted specific competitor monthly bills and a "$0" total. SyncForge removes the managed-database bill; it does not remove the cost of a signaling server or a TURN relay. Check current vendor pricing rather than trusting a figure in a text file.
- **There are no "SDK packages".** The repository is the distribution.

## Real exported symbols

Verified by importing the built module:

- `SyncForge` — main database class
- `Collection` — document collection
- `Query` — chainable query builder
- `SyncManager` — coordinates peer sync
- `VectorClock` — per-peer logical clock
- `LWWRegister`, `LWWMap` — last-writer-wins register and map
- `ORSet` — observed-remove set
- `GCounter`, `PNCounter` — grow-only and increment/decrement counters
- `IndexedDBAdapter`, `MemoryAdapter` — storage adapters
- `EventEmitter` — event bus

`WebRTCTransport` is **not** exported; it is an internal detail reached through `SyncManager`.

**Symbols that do NOT exist** (they appeared in earlier documentation and throw `TypeError`): `SyncForge.Document`, `SyncForge.WebRTCProvider`, `SyncForge.PNCounter` as a namespace member, `db.update()`, `db.subscribe()`.

## Integration recipe

```javascript
import { SyncForge } from 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/itsoumya-d/syncforge@main/dist/index.mjs';

const db = new SyncForge({ dbName: 'my-app' });   // dbName is required
const tasks = db.collection('tasks');

await tasks.set('task-1', { title: 'Write tests', done: false });
const task = await tasks.get('task-1');
const open = await tasks.where('done', '==', false).orderBy('title').limit(10).get();
await tasks.increment('task-1', 'views', 1);

const unsubscribe = tasks.subscribe((docs) => render(docs));

db.on('online', () => {});             // a peer data channel opened
db.on('offline', () => {});            // the last peer channel closed
db.on('peer-unreachable', (i) => {});  // ICE failed for a peer (no TURN configured)
db.on('signaling-failed', (i) => {});  // signaling unreachable after 5 attempts (~31 s)
db.on('error', (e) => {});
db.connectPeer('wss://your-signaling-server.example');
db.isOnline();                          // false until a peer channel actually opens
```

## Consistency properties

The merge algebra is property-tested in `tests/crdt-properties.test.mjs`, which needs no network:

- `LWWRegister`, `LWWMap`, `GCounter`, `PNCounter` and `ORSet` merges are commutative, associative and idempotent over seeded random states.
- Replicas converge under randomised delivery order, and under duplicate (at-least-once) delivery, for `set` / `delete` / `increment` / `decrement`.
- LWW conflicts are resolved by a total order on (timestamp, peerId, value). The value term is required because `Date.now()` has 1 ms granularity, so ties between same-peer writes are common.
- **Dropped operations are not recovered.** There is no anti-entropy protocol. If a frame is lost, the replicas stay divergent.
- `LWWMap` caps a map at 10 000 keys as a state-bomb mitigation. Two replicas that reach the cap having learned different keys will not converge.

## Measured performance (Node 24, MemoryAdapter, 1000 iterations)

| Operation | total | per op |
|---|---|---|
| `col.set()` across 1000 distinct documents | ~20 ms | ~0.020 ms |
| `col.get()` across 1000 distinct documents | ~1 ms | ~0.001 ms |

One caveat materially changes that picture: writes to a **single** document are O(n²), because each operation rebuilds that document's whole LWW map from stored metadata. Measured on the same machine: 250 writes to one document = 0.14 ms/op; 1000 writes = 0.37 ms/op; 4000 writes = 1.64 ms/op (6.5 s total). Collaborative editing of one document is the slow path, not the fast one. P2P sync latency is network-dependent and is not measured here.
